programs.tagline: Save on camping, day passes, and cabin rentals at all Wyoming state parks and historic sites if your loved one is 62+

localEntities.name: All Wyoming State Parks, Historic Sites, & Trails locations.

programs.intro:
If your Wyoming loved one is 62 or older, they automatically qualify for reduced fees at all Wyoming state parks and historic sites, no application needed. They'll pay less for day-use passes, camping spots, cabin rentals, and entry to historic sites like Fort Laramie and Devils Tower.

Because there's no formal senior pass to purchase, your loved one simply shows their photo ID and proof of Wyoming residency at the park entrance to receive the discount. This works at all 35+ state parks and historic sites across Wyoming, from Curt Gowdy State Park to Hot Springs State Park.

This discount is separate from the federal Senior Pass for national parks like Yellowstone, that's a different program with different requirements. Wyoming's program is specifically for state-run parks and historic sites.

faqs.question: Does this work at Yellowstone and other national parks in Wyoming?

faqs.question: What if my loved one is a Wyoming resident but doesn't have a Wyoming driver's license?

faqs.question: Can my out-of-state loved one get this discount when visiting me in Wyoming?
faqs.answer: No, this benefit is only for Wyoming residents. Your loved one would need to establish Wyoming residency to qualify. Out-of-state visitors pay regular non-resident rates at Wyoming state parks.

faqs.question: Do I need to reapply or renew this discount annually?
faqs.answer: No, there's no pass to purchase or renew. As long as your loved one remains a Wyoming resident and is 62+, they simply show their documents each visit to receive the discount. No paperwork or annual fees required.

programs.name: Low Income Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
programs.tagline: Help paying winter heating bills, up to $2,176 per year for qualifying Wyoming families.

localEntities.name: Statewide contractors (e.g., NOWCAP); contact (800) 246-4221 for local

programs.intro:
If your loved one struggles to pay heating bills during Wyoming's harsh winters, LIHEAP can provide direct payment to their utility company. This federal program pays between $49 and $2,176 toward heating costs from November through May, with the payment going straight to the utility so your loved one doesn't have to manage reimbursements.

Your loved one qualifies if their household income is below $2,985/month for a single person or $3,904/month for a couple. Because Wyoming uses automatic eligibility, if your loved one already receives SNAP, SSI, TANF, or certain veterans benefits, they're immediately approved without income verification.

Crisis assistance provides an additional $550 in winter months if your loved one faces shut-off notices or heating system failures. Applications open October 1st each year, but funding is limited and the program often closes early when money runs out.

faqs.question: What if my loved one lives with other family members who don't help pay utilities?
faqs.answer: Everyone living at the same address counts as one household for LIEAP purposes, even if they keep separate finances. You'll need to include income from all household members when applying, which may affect eligibility if their combined income exceeds the limits.

faqs.question: Can I apply for both regular heating assistance and crisis assistance?
faqs.answer: Yes, but you must complete the regular LIEAP application first. Crisis assistance provides up to an additional $550 in winter months for shut-off notices or heating failures, but it's separate from the regular $49-$2,176 heating benefit.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's utility company threatens shut-off before I can get crisis help?
faqs.answer: Contact (800) 246-4221 immediately and explain the emergency situation. Crisis assistance is designed for these situations, but you must have the regular LIEAP application on file first. Many utility companies will delay shut-off if you can show a pending LIEAP application.

faqs.question: How do I know if my loved one qualifies for automatic eligibility?
faqs.answer: If your loved one receives SNAP food benefits, SSI, TANF, or certain veterans benefits, they automatically qualify without income verification. Bring their benefit award letter or card when applying to streamline the process.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply if they heat with propane or wood instead of electric or gas?
faqs.answer: Yes, LIEAP covers various heating fuel types including propane. The program pays vendors directly, so your loved one will need bills or receipts from their propane supplier or other fuel vendor.

faqs.question: What if we miss the application deadline because the program closes early?
faqs.answer: If LIEAP funding runs out before April 30th, there's no additional funding until the next heating season starting October 1st. This is why applying as early as possible in October is crucial, waiting until winter arrives often means missing out entirely.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one who has trouble with paperwork?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can help with the application process. When you call (800) 246-4221, explain that you're helping your loved one apply and ask about any authorization forms needed to discuss their case with the regional contractor.

faqs.question: Will LIEAP assistance affect my loved one's other benefits like Medicaid or Social Security?
faqs.answer: No, LIEAP payments go directly to utility companies and don't count as income for other benefit programs. Since the money never goes to your loved one directly, it won't affect Social Security, Medicaid, or other assistance programs they receive.

programs.name: Wyoming Tax Refund for Elderly & Disabled
programs.tagline: Annual refunds of $250–900 to help Wyoming seniors cover property taxes and utility costs.
programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ or permanently disabled and lives in Wyoming on a fixed income, they may qualify for an annual tax refund of $250–900. Because Wyoming doesn't have state income tax, this program refunds money your loved one paid through sales taxes, property taxes, and utility costs throughout the year.

The refund amount depends on your loved one's income level. Single applicants with income below $10,000 receive the full $800 refund, while those earning $10,001–$17,500 get a prorated amount down to $250. Married couples get $900 (full refund) if their combined income is below $16,000, prorated down to $216 for incomes up to $28,500.

Your loved one must reapply every year and meet asset limits of $29,950 per adult household member. The program is administered by the Wyoming Department of Health and available statewide to qualifying residents.

faqs.question: Can I apply for my loved one if they have dementia or can't handle paperwork?
faqs.answer: The sources don't specify whether family members can apply on behalf of elderly or disabled parents. Contact the Wyoming Department of Health directly to ask about representative payee or power of attorney arrangements for the application process.

faqs.question: What counts toward the $29,950 asset limit per person?
faqs.answer: The sources don't detail which assets are counted or exempted from the limit. Your loved one's home may or may not count toward this limit. Contact Wyoming Department of Health for a complete list of countable assets before applying.

faqs.question: If my loved one moves to Wyoming from another state, when can they apply?
faqs.answer: Your loved one must be a Wyoming resident for 12 consecutive months before applying. If they moved to Wyoming in January, they couldn't apply until the following January at the earliest.

faqs.question: How much will my loved one actually receive if their income is in the middle range?
faqs.answer: Refunds are prorated between the minimum and maximum amounts based on income. For example, if your single loved one earns $13,750 (halfway between $10,000-$17,500), they'd likely receive around $525 (halfway between $250-$800). Contact Wyoming Department of Health for the exact calculation formula.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one forgets to reapply one year?
faqs.answer: They lose eligibility for that year since this requires a new application annually. There's no automatic renewal or carryover from previous years. They can reapply the following year if still eligible.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get both this refund and the Property Tax Refund Program?
faqs.answer: These are separate programs with different administrators and eligibility rules. The Property Tax Refund Program is run by the Department of Revenue and has different requirements like 5-year residency. Contact both agencies to see if your loved one qualifies for both.

programs.name: Aged, Blind, and Disabled Medicaid
programs.tagline: If your parent is 65 or older, blind, or disabled and living in Wyoming, this program can cover doctor visits, prescriptions, nursing home care, and home-based services at little or no cost.

localEntities.name: Wyoming Department of Health Customer Service Center, 3001 E. Pershing Blvd., Suite 125, Cheyenne, WY 82001

programs.intro:
Wyoming's Aged, Blind, and Disabled (ABD) Medicaid pays for medical care that Medicare either doesn't cover or only partially covers: doctor visits, hospital stays, prescriptions, behavioral health, dental (two preventive and two emergency visits per year), long-term nursing facility care, and home and community-based services that let your parent stay out of a facility. If your parent is already on Supplemental Security Income (SSI), they likely qualify automatically. If they're not on SSI but are 65 or older, blind, or disabled with limited income and assets, they may still qualify through one of several ABD pathways.

This is not a single program with one income limit. Wyoming runs multiple ABD coverage groups with different eligibility rules. The main divide is between SSI-related eligibility (which follows federal SSI income and resource standards) and institutional or waiver-related eligibility (which generally allows income up to 300% of the Federal Benefit Rate, a higher threshold designed for people who need nursing home or home-based care). Which pathway fits your parent determines what limits apply, so the first step is identifying the right category before comparing numbers.

Routine vision care is not covered except to treat an eye disease or injury. Dental coverage exists but is capped. Beyond those limits, this program covers a broad range of medical and long-term care services, and for many families it is the most important coverage their parent can hold. Apply as soon as you think your parent may qualify; the state does not automatically enroll people who are eligible.

contentSections.title: Two different income rules: which one applies to your parent?
contentSections.body:
SSI-related ABD: Applies to people who receive SSI or who qualify under federal SSI income and resource standards. This is the baseline pathway for aged, blind, or disabled individuals not seeking institutional or waiver-based care.

Institutional or waiver-related ABD: Applies to people who need nursing facility care or Home and Community Based Services through a waiver. Income can be higher under this pathway, generally up to 300% of the Federal Benefit Rate. A clinical level-of-care assessment is also required. If your parent's income is too high for SSI-related eligibility, they may still qualify under this track.

contentSections.title: What ABD Medicaid does and does not cover
contentSections.body:
Covered: Doctor visits, outpatient and inpatient hospital care, prescriptions, behavioral health, non-emergency medical transportation, screenings, two preventive dental visits per year, two emergency dental visits per year, nursing facility care, and home and community-based waiver services.

Not covered: Routine vision care (glasses, routine exams). Vision coverage is limited to treatment of an eye disease or injury. Dental coverage is capped at the visit limits above, not unlimited.

If your parent also has Medicare, ABD Medicaid often acts as secondary coverage, paying costs Medicare leaves behind such as copays and deductibles.

faqs.question: My parent owns their home. Does that disqualify them?
faqs.answer: The primary home is generally exempt from the resource count under Wyoming ABD Medicaid, meaning it is not counted against your parent when the state evaluates their assets. However, exemption conditions apply, and the state's eligibility manual contains the controlling rules. Call 1-855-294-2127 or consult Wyoming's Medicaid eligibility manual at health.wyo.gov to confirm how the home is treated for your parent's specific coverage group. For nursing facility coverage, there are also estate recovery rules that may apply after your parent's death; ask about those separately.

faqs.question: My parent's income is too high for SSI. Does that mean they can't get ABD Medicaid at all?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Wyoming has a separate ABD pathway for people who need nursing facility care or Home and Community Based Services through a waiver, and that pathway allows income up to 300% of the Federal Benefit Rate, which is higher than the SSI income limit. If your parent needs significant daily care, they may qualify under this institutional or waiver track even if standard SSI-related Medicaid is out of reach. Call 1-855-294-2127 and ask specifically about the institutional or HCBS waiver pathway.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly parent if they can't do it themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member, legal guardian, or authorized representative can apply on your parent's behalf. You will need documentation showing your authority to act for them, such as a power of attorney, guardianship order, or a signed representative authorization form. Submit that documentation along with the application. If you're unsure which document you need, call 1-855-294-2127 before you apply.

faqs.question: How is disability determined if my parent has never applied for SSI or Social Security disability?
faqs.answer: If the Social Security Administration has not already made a disability determination for your parent, the Wyoming Department of Health will evaluate disability using SSA's standards. This requires medical records, physician documentation, and evidence of your parent's functional limitations. The process takes additional time beyond the standard financial eligibility review. Submit complete medical documentation when you apply to avoid back-and-forth delays.

faqs.question: Can my parent get both Medicare and ABD Medicaid at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. People who have both are called dual eligibles. When your parent has Medicare, ABD Medicaid typically acts as secondary coverage, paying costs Medicare doesn't cover such as deductibles, copays, and some services Medicare excludes. If your parent qualifies for both, a Medicare Savings Program may also help pay Medicare premiums; ask about those programs at the same time you apply for ABD Medicaid.

faqs.question: What happens if my parent's income or health status changes after they're enrolled?
faqs.answer: Wyoming requires enrollees to report changes in income, resources, living situation, or health status. The state conducts periodic redeterminations to confirm continued eligibility. If your parent's condition worsens and they now need nursing facility or waiver-level care, contact 1-855-294-2127 to discuss whether a different ABD coverage group or a level-of-care assessment is appropriate. Changes in income or assets can affect which pathway they qualify under.

faqs.question: Is there a waitlist for ABD Medicaid itself?
faqs.answer: No statewide waitlist for ABD Medicaid was identified in official Wyoming materials. However, specific Home and Community Based Services waiver programs have their own administration and may have access limitations based on provider availability and level-of-care determinations. When you apply, ask specifically whether the particular waiver services your parent needs have any waiting period or availability constraints.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for ABD Medicaid and a Medicare Savings Program at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is worth doing both at once. Medicare Savings Programs help pay Medicare Part A and Part B premiums, deductibles, and copays. ABD Medicaid covers a broader range of services. Applying for both at the same time through Wyoming's Customer Service Center at 1-855-294-2127 or at wesystem.wyo.gov can help your parent maximize coverage without duplicating the paperwork effort.

programs.intro:
Wyoming's Community Choice Waiver (CCW) is a Medicaid program that pays for home and community-based services so your parent can get nursing-home-level care without moving into a nursing facility. If a trained public health nurse has determined your parent needs daily help with things like bathing, dressing, or medication management, CCW can cover services including personal care aides, home-delivered meals, adult day programs, respite for you as a caregiver, skilled nursing visits, assistive technology, and home modifications.

This is not a cash benefit. CCW covers a specific menu of services coordinated through a case management agency your parent chooses after enrollment. That agency becomes the central point of contact for arranging and adjusting care over time, so your parent is not left managing multiple providers alone.

CCW is open statewide to Wyoming residents age 65 and older, and to adults ages 19 to 64 with a verified disability. To qualify, your parent must meet Wyoming Medicaid financial eligibility requirements and pass a functional assessment (called the LT-101) confirming they need nursing facility level of care. The financial threshold is set at 300% of the Federal Benefit Rate; the dollar amount changes each year, so verifying the current limit directly with Wyoming's Benefits and Eligibility Specialist for your area is essential.
programs.savingsSource: Free service: CCW covers home and community-based services at no premium cost to eligible Medicaid recipients. Dollar value varies by the services authorized in the individual care plan; Wyoming Department of Health does not publish a universal per-person cap.

contentSections.title: What CCW actually pays for
contentSections.body: CCW is not a cash program. It pays directly for services your parent's case manager authorizes in the care plan. Covered services include: personal support services (help with bathing, dressing, meals), home health aide visits, skilled nursing visits, adult day programs, home-delivered meals, non-medical transportation, companion services, respite care (giving you a break as a caregiver), assistive technology, home modifications (ramps, grab bars, widened doorways), personal emergency response systems (PERS), and case management itself. The specific services and hours your parent receives depend on what the LT-101 assessment shows and what the care plan authorizes.

contentSections.title: The two gates every applicant must pass
contentSections.body:
CCW has two separate eligibility gates, and your parent must clear both.

Gate 1 is financial: your parent must qualify for Wyoming Medicaid. Income must generally be at or below 300% of the Federal Benefit Rate (the exact dollar amount changes annually). Countable resources are reviewed under Medicaid-style rules. Assets like the primary home and one vehicle are typically exempt, but the full asset review happens during Medicaid enrollment.

Gate 2 is functional: a trained public health nurse must assess your parent using Wyoming's LT-101 tool and determine that your parent needs nursing facility level of care. This means your parent requires substantial daily assistance with tasks like bathing, dressing, eating, moving around, or managing medications. If your parent does not pass the LT-101, they are not eligible for CCW regardless of income.

Both gates must be cleared before services begin, and the functional assessment is repeated at least every year.

faqs.question: My parent wants to stay in their home. Does CCW actually make that possible, or does it require moving somewhere?
faqs.answer: CCW is specifically designed to help people stay in their homes or in community settings instead of moving to a nursing facility. Covered services like personal care aides, home modifications, home-delivered meals, and skilled nursing visits all come to where your parent lives. Some participants also use adult day programs while continuing to live at home. If your parent's care needs eventually exceed what can be safely provided at home, the case manager will talk with your family about other options.

faqs.question: My parent is already in a nursing facility. Can they use CCW to move back home?
faqs.answer: Yes. CCW includes Transition Intensive Case Management and Transition Setup Services specifically to help people move out of nursing facilities and back into the community. If your parent is currently in a facility, ask the facility's social worker to connect you with a Wyoming CCW Benefits and Eligibility Specialist, or call 307-630-4729 directly. The transition services can help fund setup costs like first-month deposits and basic household items.

faqs.question: Can I, as the caregiver, get any help through CCW, or is everything for my parent?
faqs.answer: CCW includes respite care, which is a service designed to give family caregivers a break. Respite allows another trained caregiver to step in so you can rest, handle other responsibilities, or simply take time for yourself. Companion services are also covered. Speak with the case manager about including respite in your parent's care plan.

faqs.question: What happens if my parent's health declines after they are enrolled? Does coverage change?
faqs.answer: The LT-101 level of care assessment is repeated at least once a year, and the care plan can be updated more frequently if your parent's needs change significantly. You can contact the case management agency at any time to request a reassessment or modification to the care plan. If your parent's needs eventually exceed what CCW can cover in the community, the case manager will discuss nursing facility placement and Medicaid coverage for that setting.

faqs.question: My parent is 58 years old with a serious disability. Can they still qualify?
faqs.answer: CCW is open to adults ages 19 to 64 with a qualifying disability, in addition to adults 65 and older. For ages 19 to 64, the disability must be verified either through a Social Security Administration disability determination letter or through a Wyoming Department of Health review using SSA criteria. If your parent does not yet have an SSA determination, you can still start the CCW application process while that documentation is being gathered.

faqs.question: Can I apply for CCW and Wyoming Medicaid at the same time, or do I have to get Medicaid first?
faqs.answer: You should apply for both at the same time. The CCW Application and the Wyoming Medicaid application can be submitted together. Submitting them separately slows things down because CCW eligibility cannot be finalized until Medicaid financial eligibility is confirmed. Download both forms from the HCBS Document Library at https://health.wyo.gov/healthcarefin/hcbs/document-library/ and submit them together.

faqs.question: How long will it take before my parent actually starts receiving services?
faqs.answer: Wyoming does not publish an official statewide processing-time target for CCW. Timing depends on how quickly the Medicaid financial review is completed, when the LT-101 assessment can be scheduled, and how soon a case management agency can begin developing the care plan. These factors vary by county. When you call 307-630-4729, ask the Benefits and Eligibility Specialist what the current typical timeframe is in your area.

faqs.question: Will CCW pay a family member to provide care, or only outside providers?
faqs.answer: CCW benefits are paid to authorized service providers through the case management structure, not directly to family members in most circumstances. Whether a family member can be hired as a paid provider under certain CCW service categories depends on program rules and case manager guidance. Ask your case management agency specifically about this when selecting your care plan options; the answer depends on the service type and your parent's situation.

programs.intro:
If your parent is on Medicare and their monthly income is below roughly $1,800 (single person), Wyoming may pay some or all of their Medicare costs. Depending on income, that means the state covers their Part B premium ($185/month in 2025), and at the highest level of help, also their deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. That is real money: the Part B premium alone adds up to over $2,200 a year.

Wyoming runs three tiers of this benefit. The lowest-income tier (QMB) pays the most: it covers premiums plus out-of-pocket cost-sharing. The middle tier (SLMB) and top tier (QI) both pay only the Part B premium. Which tier your parent qualifies for depends on their countable income, which is not always the same as their gross income. Some income is excluded by rule.

This program is often missed because families assume Medicare covers everything, or because the three-tier structure is confusing. It does not require your parent to give up their current doctors. Enrollment runs through Wyoming's Medicaid office, not Medicare itself.

faqs.question: My parent already has Medicare. Do they have to change their plan or doctors to get this benefit?
faqs.answer: No. Medicare Savings Programs pay costs within your parent's existing Medicare coverage. They keep their current Medicare card, their current doctors, and any Medicare Advantage or supplement plan they already have. This is a payment program, not a new insurance plan.

faqs.question: My parent's Social Security check is $1,600/month. Does that automatically disqualify them from QMB?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Wyoming uses countable income, not simply the gross Social Security amount. Some income is excluded under Social Security Administration rules before the comparison to the limit is made. Ask the application worker to calculate countable income before assuming your parent is over the QMB limit of $1,330/month. They may still qualify for SLMB ($1,596 limit) or QI ($1,796 limit).

faqs.question: What is the asset limit and does my parent's house count against it?
faqs.answer: Wyoming applies a resource (asset) limit tied to Social Security Administration rules and adjusted annually. The official Wyoming program pages did not publish the full list of exempt assets in the materials we reviewed. Before applying, ask the application worker whether your parent's home, vehicle, and personal property are exempt. Do not assume your parent is ineligible because of assets without getting the worker's assessment first.

faqs.question: My parent already tried to get SLMB and was told their income is too high. Should they try again for QI?
faqs.answer: Yes. QI's income limit ($1,796/month for a single person) is $200 higher than SLMB's. It is the most commonly overlooked tier. Ask the worker specifically to screen for QI. The benefit is the same as SLMB (Part B premium paid), and the application is identical. Note that QI funding is capped federally and renewed each year, so applying early in the calendar year improves chances.

faqs.question: Can I apply for Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help (the Part D drug subsidy) at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. QMB, SLMB, and QI enrollment automatically qualifies your parent for Extra Help, which reduces their Medicare Part D prescription drug costs. You do not need a separate application for Extra Help once MSP is approved. Social Security applies it automatically. If your parent is not yet on MSP, apply for Extra Help directly through Social Security at 800-772-1213 while the MSP application is pending.

faqs.question: A provider billed my parent even though they are enrolled in QMB. Is that allowed?
faqs.answer: No. Federal law prohibits providers who accept Medicare from billing QMB enrollees for Medicare deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments. If a bill arrives, remind the provider of your parent's QMB status in writing. If the provider continues billing, you can file a complaint through your State Medical Assistance office or call Medicare at 800-MEDICARE (800-633-4227).

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly parent if they cannot manage the paperwork themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member, legal representative, or authorized representative can apply on behalf of a Medicare beneficiary. Tell the application worker at the start of the call that you are applying as the representative. You may need to provide your own ID and contact information in addition to your parent's documents.

faqs.question: How do we know if approval actually goes through and the premium gets removed?
faqs.answer: After Wyoming approves the application, the state sends the information to the Social Security Administration, which adjusts the Part B premium deduction from your parent's Social Security check. This adjustment can take up to 60 days. Check the next two Social Security deposit amounts. If the premium is still being deducted after 60 days, call Social Security at 800-772-1213 and reference the MSP approval.

programs.intro:
If your parent is 60 or older and struggling to afford groceries on a fixed income, Wyoming SNAP may help. Benefits are loaded monthly onto an EBT card (a debit card that works at most grocery stores and many farmers markets), with maximums of $306/month for a single person and $562/month for a two-person household, for the period October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027. The actual amount depends on your parent's household size, income, and certain deductions.

Wyoming gives households with an elderly or disabled member a higher income threshold than it gives working-age households. That matters if your parent's gross monthly income is between $1,730 and $2,195 for a one-person household: a working-age applicant would be denied, but your parent may still qualify. Even if gross income is under that limit, Wyoming also applies a net-income test after deductions, including a deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses that many families miss.

Applying in Wyoming is not a single online click. The process involves submitting a paper or email application, then scheduling a phone or in-person interview with a benefit specialist at your local Department of Family Services (DFS) office. An asset test also applies, though the exact dollar threshold was not published in the official sources retrieved; you will need to confirm the current counted-resource limit with DFS before applying. The sections below walk through income rules, documents, and how to start.

applicationGuide.tip: Claim the medical-expense deduction. Many families skip it. Ask the benefit specialist about this during the interview.

applicationNotes: Wyoming does not appear to use Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility, which means an asset test applies even for households with elderly or disabled members. Confirm the current counted-resource dollar limit with your local DFS office before applying, because the exact figure was not published in the official sources we reviewed.

If your parent has an urgent food need, ask the DFS benefit specialist about expedited processing. Federal rules require expedited SNAP benefits within 7 days for households with very low income or resources; ask whether your parent qualifies when you call.

The medical-expense deduction is available to households with a member age 60 or older or who is disabled. Out-of-pocket costs for prescriptions, doctor visits, dental care, and medical equipment can reduce countable net income, which can both establish eligibility and increase the monthly benefit. Many families do not claim this deduction.
Answer all calls from DFS after submitting the application. The interview cannot be completed without your response, and an unanswered interview request can result in the application being closed.

contentSections.title: The income rule that matters most for older adults
contentSections.body: Wyoming has two gross-income thresholds. For working-age households, the limit is 130% of the federal poverty level ($1,729/month for one person in FY2026-27). For households with a member who is 60 or older or disabled, the limit rises to 165% of poverty ($2,195/month for one person). This higher threshold is why your parent may qualify even if a neighbor of the same household size was denied. Both groups must also pass the net-income test ($1,330/month for one person), which is calculated after deductions including the medical-expense deduction described above.

contentSections.title: What SNAP benefits can and cannot buy
contentSections.body: EBT benefits pay for most grocery store food items: fruits, vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, dairy, bread, cereals, and non-alcoholic beverages. They also cover seeds and plants that produce food. They cannot be used for alcohol, tobacco, vitamins and supplements sold separately, hot prepared foods, or non-food household items. Most major grocery chains in Wyoming accept EBT. Many farmers markets do as well; look for the EBT sign or ask the vendor.

contentSections.title: The asset test: what we know and what you need to confirm
contentSections.body: Wyoming SNAP applies a resource test that counts liquid assets like cash and bank account balances. The primary home is excluded. Most retirement accounts are also excluded, but you should confirm this with DFS for your parent's specific account types. Because the official sources we reviewed did not publish the exact current dollar asset limit, we cannot state it here. Before your parent applies, call your local DFS office and ask: 'What is the current countable resource limit for a household with an elderly member, and what accounts or assets do you count?' That one question will tell you whether an asset issue exists before you invest time in the full application.

faqs.question: My parent's Social Security check is just over $1,729/month. Does that automatically disqualify them?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Wyoming uses a higher gross-income threshold of $2,195/month for households with a member who is 60 or older or disabled. If your parent's income is between $1,730 and $2,195, they may still qualify under the elderly/disabled rule. They also must pass a separate net-income test at $1,330/month, but that is calculated after deductions including medical expenses, which can meaningfully lower the counted figure.

faqs.question: Can I apply for SNAP on behalf of my elderly parent if they cannot manage the process themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. An authorized representative can complete and submit the application on your parent's behalf. Inform the DFS benefit specialist during the interview that you are acting as the authorized representative. DFS may ask for written confirmation of that arrangement. The interview can often be conducted by phone, which makes it more manageable for a caregiver coordinating from a distance.

faqs.question: My parent owns their home and has a small savings account. Will the asset test disqualify them?
faqs.answer: The primary home is excluded from the SNAP resource count. A savings account balance is generally counted. Because the official Wyoming DFS sources we reviewed did not publish the exact current asset limit, we cannot give you a precise number to compare against. Call your local DFS office before applying and ask for the current countable-resource limit for a household with an elderly or disabled member. That answer takes about two minutes to get and tells you whether the savings account is a problem.

faqs.question: My parent pays a lot out of pocket for prescriptions and doctor visits. Does that help with SNAP?
faqs.answer: Yes. Federal SNAP rules allow a medical-expense deduction for households with a member who is 60 or older or disabled. Out-of-pocket costs for prescriptions, doctor visits, dental care, vision, and medical equipment can be deducted when calculating net income. This deduction is one of the most commonly missed by families. Bring documentation of those costs to the interview and ask the benefit specialist to apply the deduction.

faqs.question: How long will it take to get a decision after we apply?
faqs.answer: The official Wyoming DFS sources we reviewed did not state a standard statewide processing-time guarantee. Processing depends on how quickly the interview is scheduled and how fast documents are verified at the local office. If your parent has an urgent food need (very low income or resources), ask about expedited processing when you contact DFS; federal rules require expedited benefits within 7 days for qualifying households. For everyone else, follow up with your local office if you have not heard back within two weeks of submitting the application.

faqs.question: Can my parent receive SNAP and LIEAP (energy assistance) at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. SNAP and Wyoming's Low Income Energy Assistance Program (LIEAP) are separate programs with separate eligibility rules. Receiving one does not disqualify your parent from the other. Many low-income older adults qualify for both. Apply for each through its own process: SNAP through DFS, and LIEAP through the Wyoming Department of Family Services energy assistance program.

faqs.question: What happens to my parent's benefit if their income or household situation changes?
faqs.answer: Your parent is required to report certain changes to DFS, such as a significant change in income or household size. Benefit amounts are recalculated when changes are reported or when DFS conducts a periodic renewal. If income drops, benefits may increase. If income rises above the limit, benefits stop. Ask DFS at the interview how often recertification is required and what changes must be reported promptly.

faqs.question: Can my parent use SNAP benefits at farmers markets or only at grocery stores?
faqs.answer: Many Wyoming farmers markets accept EBT, but not all. Look for an EBT sign at the market or ask a vendor before assuming. Major grocery chains statewide accept EBT. Benefits cannot be used for hot prepared foods, alcohol, tobacco, or non-food items regardless of where your parent shops.

programs.tagline: If your parent is 60+ and can't easily prepare their own meals, Wyoming may deliver nutritious meals directly to their home at no cost, regardless of income.

programs.intro:
Wyoming's Home-Delivered Meals program sends meals directly to your parent's home if they are 60 or older and cannot easily prepare food themselves. This is not an income-based program: there is no financial means test. What matters is your parent's age, their functional need, and whether they are homebound or otherwise unable to get to a group meal site.

The program typically delivers meals five days a week. In some rural parts of Wyoming, daily delivery is not always possible, and a reduced schedule may be approved. Meals may be hot, cold, frozen, canned, or supplemental foods depending on the county provider. This is a free service. Some providers may ask for a voluntary contribution, but payment is never required and is never a condition of receiving meals.

Because the program is run county by county through local aging services providers, who you call and how quickly you get started depends on where your parent lives. The first step is finding the right local contact, which you can do through the Wyoming Department of Health's county service-area map.

This looks at your parent's nutritional risk, ability to prepare food, and homebound status. Have basic information ready: your parent's age, current living situation, and any medical or functional limitations that affect meal preparation.

steps.title: Confirm enrollment and delivery schedule
steps.description: Once the assessment is complete and your parent qualifies, the local provider will confirm the delivery schedule. In most of Wyoming this is five days per week. If your parent lives in a rural area, ask specifically about delivery frequency, since a reduced schedule may apply.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No statewide processing-time standard is published. Timing depends on the local county provider's assessment schedule and current capacity.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No formal statewide waitlist policy was identified in official Wyoming materials. Availability and any delays vary by county and local provider capacity. Ask your local provider directly about current wait times when you call.
applicationGuide.tip: When you call, mention any medical conditions or recent hospital stays that affect your parent's ability to cook. This information is relevant to the AGNES assessment and may affect priority placement.

applicationNotes: Because each county runs its own intake process, wait times and delivery frequency can differ significantly depending on where your parent lives. Always ask the local provider about current capacity when you first call.

If your parent lives in a rural area, ask specifically whether five-day-per-week delivery is available in their location. A reduced schedule may be the only option, and it is worth knowing this upfront before enrollment.

contentSections.title: No income test. No asset test.
contentSections.body: Many families assume their parent earns too much or owns too much to qualify. Wyoming's Home-Delivered Meals program is funded under the Older Americans Act and does not use income or assets as eligibility criteria. Age and functional need are the only gates. Source: https://health.wyo.gov/aging/communityliving/older-americans-act-programs/nutrition/

contentSections.title: What kinds of meals are delivered?
contentSections.body: Meals are not always hot. Depending on your county's provider and delivery model, your parent may receive hot meals, cold meals, frozen meals, canned goods, fresh food, or supplemental nutrition products. The format depends on what the local provider operates. Ask when you call what format is standard in your county.

contentSections.title: Rural Wyoming: what to expect
contentSections.body: Wyoming's official program materials acknowledge that five-day-per-week delivery is standard, but that a lesser frequency may be approved in rural areas where daily delivery is not feasible. If your parent lives in a sparsely populated county, delivery may come two or three times per week rather than daily. Ask the local provider what the actual schedule looks like for your parent's address before you complete the AGNES assessment.

faqs.question: My parent has retirement income and owns their home. Do they still qualify?
faqs.answer: Yes. Wyoming's Home-Delivered Meals program has no income limit and no asset limit. Eligibility is based on age (60+), the inability to prepare meals, and homebound status. Your parent's retirement income and home ownership are not factors in the decision.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent if they can't make calls themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. Family members and caregivers routinely initiate contact on behalf of an older parent. Call (307) 777-5048 or reach your county provider through the service-area map at https://health.wyo.gov/aging/communityliving/service-area-maps/. You will want to have your parent's basic information ready, including their address, age, and a description of their functional limitations.

faqs.question: How long will it take to start receiving meals after we apply?
faqs.answer: Wyoming does not publish a statewide processing-time standard. The timeline depends on your county provider's assessment schedule and current capacity. Some counties may start delivery within days of the AGNES assessment; others may take longer. Ask the local provider directly when you call: 'How quickly can you schedule the assessment, and how long after that before delivery starts?'

faqs.question: What if my parent's condition changes after they're enrolled?
faqs.answer: Notify the local county provider if your parent's living situation, health, or ability to prepare meals changes significantly. The AGNES tool is used for the initial assessment, but providers can conduct follow-up evaluations. Changes in need may affect delivery frequency or the type of meals provided.

faqs.question: Will my parent be charged for the meals?
faqs.answer: No. This is a free service. Some local providers may offer the option to make a voluntary contribution, but payment is never required and cannot be used as a condition for receiving or continuing meals. If any provider suggests otherwise, contact the Wyoming Department of Health Aging Division at (307) 777-5048.

faqs.question: My parent lives in a very rural county. Will they actually get meals delivered?
faqs.answer: The program is available statewide, but delivery frequency in rural areas may be lower than the standard five days per week. Wyoming's official materials state that a reduced frequency can be approved when daily delivery is not feasible. Contact your county provider through the service-area map at https://health.wyo.gov/aging/communityliving/service-area-maps/ and ask specifically what delivery looks like at your parent's address.

stateOverview.intro: Wyoming offers 3 key programs to help seniors with living costs, from reducing state park fees to covering heating bills and providing tax relief. These programs can save your loved one $250–2,176 per year, depending on their income and needs. Most have simple applications through state agencies, and one requires no application at all. Start with the programs that address your loved one's biggest expenses: heating costs in Wyoming's harsh winters, property taxes, or recreation if they're active outdoors.
